_what_this_is: THE STRUCTURAL PIECE KIT. Six pieces. A player places these on the deck grid and a
deckhouse emerges from the placements; nobody ever types a corner coordinate and nobody
ever describes a room and has it materialise at a custom size.
THE SPLIT. `plate`, `spar`, `wire`, `sheer_band` are the BAKING layer - general geometry,
already proven, unchanged by this file. This is the AUTHORING layer: a piece is a named
thing with a footprint in CELLS that RESOLVES into those primitives. StructureBaker never
learns a new word.
THE RULE THAT MAKES THIS MINECRAFT AND NOT CAD, and every entry below obeys it:
EVERY PARAMETER TAKES ITS VALUE FROM A DECLARED FINITE SET, AND EVERY GEOMETRIC
PARAMETER IS COUNTED IN GRID UNITS.
Extents - span, depth, height, sill, band - are whole CELLS (0.5 m). The five parameters
that TRIM a piece off the whole-cell lattice - rake, head, fall, lift, offset - are whole
EIGHTH-CELLS (0.125 m). Openings, gauges and profiles are named choices. No float is ever
typed by a player, so two pieces placed side by side meet exactly - which is the property
a kit lives or dies on.
A NAMING DEFECT, INHERITED AND KEPT. `quarter_cells` in version 1 meant 0.25 m, which is
HALF a cell, not a quarter; the ordinals were counting fractions of a METRE. `eighth_cells`
= 0.125 m keeps that (wrong) ordinal so the two names stay in the same series. The unit a
reader should trust is the metre value written in every `_is` below, not the name.
WHY THE TRIM STEP IS 0.125 m AND NOT 0.25 OR 0.0625, measured rather than chosen. Across
the 52 player-set wall rakes in this repo's hand-authored fleet, the worst quantisation
error is 0.110 m at a 0.25 m step, 0.062 m at 0.125 m and 0.030 m at 0.0625 m, for value
sets of 9, 17 and 33 entries spanning the same +-1.0 m. The kit's own plating is 0.10 m
thick: at a 0.25 m step the worst wall in the fleet is displaced by MORE than the material
it is made of, and at 0.125 m it is displaced by less. That is the knee, and it is the
reason the second halving - which costs 16 more entries on every stepper - is not taken.
WHY RAKE IS A PARAMETER AND NOT A SET OF FIXED VARIANTS. Covering this repo's existing
vessels with fixed rakes needs 0, 3, 7, 11, 12, 17, 20 degrees - seven variants of every
wall piece, which is seven times the thing a player has to learn for one axis of variation.
Quantising the rake to an eighth-cell of top-edge offset gives the same guarantee a fixed
set was bought for (neighbours match, no slot of daylight opens between them) at the cost
of one number picked off a seventeen-entry stepper.
WHY `head` AND `lift` EXIST, AND WHAT WOULD DELETE THEM. A placement's `cell` is whole
cells on ALL THREE axes, and that lattice is restated in `structure_plan.gd`
(`piece_node_plan`) so a document can be normalised without loading the kit. So a tier
cannot be 2.75 m tall by standing on a half-level: `head` adds eighth-cells to a wall's
TOP and `lift` moves a piece's FOOT off its node, and between them a deckhouse escapes the
0.5 m vertical lattice without the lattice moving. If `PieceKit.node_plan` and
`StructurePlan.piece_node_plan` ever move their Y to eighth-cells together, `lift` is dead
weight and should be deleted. `head` is separate from `height` for a harder reason: making
`height` count eighth-cells would HALVE every deckhouse already saved, silently, and a kit
whose pieces quietly change size is worse than one that refuses.
WHY CAMBER AND FALL LIVE ON `deck_tile` AND NOT ON `roof_slope`, AND NOT ON A NEW PIECE.
A boat deck that falls 0.25 m over 8 m is a DECK - you walk on it, it is the tier's roof,
it carries the eave. `roof_slope` is the other thing: a whaleback, a visor, a casing top
that climbs WHOLE CELLS and CHAINS with itself, and making its `rise` fine would break the
chaining that is its whole point. A seventh piece for `a deck that is 3 degrees off flat`
is a piece a player must learn to build something that is not a different object. So
`fall` is a parameter of the deck, zero by default, and a CAMBER - a crown rather than a
slope - is two tiles at the same fall placed back to back off a centreline, which meet
exactly along the crown because neither number was typed.
WHY THE CORNER IS ITS OWN PIECE, and this is the piece that beats blockiness. Two raked
walls meeting at 90 degrees do NOT meet: each top edge has moved outboard along its own
normal, so a wedge opens at the corner exactly as wide as the rake. `corner_45` is the
adapter. Its two vertical edges belong to its two neighbours and its single plate is
BILINEAR, so it absorbs any difference between the two rakes - including a raked front
meeting a plumb side, which is the trawler's whole forward end. The by-product is that a
raked house is chamfered at every corner by construction, and a chamfered corner is the
one thing a stack of square panels can never look like. CONVEX only: at a CONCAVE corner a
facet's two edges face into the reflex angle, and the transition it can carry there is zero -
feet close, heads open by exactly the neighbours' rake difference. And the version-1
instruction `placed 180 degrees round it fills a concave corner` was simply wrong by 1.74 m.
An adversarial critic's exhaustive search of 11,664 legal placements reports the working one
as the vertex plus (d_out - d_in) cells at facing(d_in) - a different cell AND a different
facing. THAT SEARCH IS NOT RE-DERIVED HERE and no test in this repo holds it, so it is
recorded as the critic's measurement and not as this file's claim; the wrong instruction is
removed either way. There is still no piece that carries a rake round an inside corner.
AND IT IS ALSO THE DIAGONAL WALL. `corner_45` spans `span` cells in X and `span` in Z, so
its chord IS a 45-degree wall segment - up to 8 cells, a 5.66 m chord, and its OUT edge is
the next facet's IN edge, so facets CHAIN into a diagonal run of any length. That is why
there is no seventh `wall_diag` piece: it would duplicate `wall_panel`'s whole parameter
surface for a wall that differs only in its plan direction. What was missing was the cap
(it was 4), the `chain` parameter and this sentence. A chained run MUST be `chain: run`:
in `chain: corner` each top corner moves along an AXIS wall's normal, and a chain of those
opens at the head by 0.125*sqrt(rake_a^2+rake_b^2) - 0.177 m at one step of rake. That
shipped, in this repo, in the fixture that was the evidence for the feature.
PLACEMENT. A piece is placed at a grid NODE (a corner between cells), not in a cell:
walls stand on cell edges. `cell` is [x, y, z] in whole cells; the piece-local frame has
+X along the run, +Y up and the OUTWARD face toward -Z; `facing` is 0/90/180/270 degrees
of yaw. Fittings - chairs, cleats, lanterns, seats - are NOT pieces and never snap: they
are `items[]` with float coordinates and PartCatalog owns them. Over half the 344 rows in
COMPONENTS.md are smaller than one cell.
WHAT THE KIT STILL REFUSES, AND WHAT IT STILL CANNOT SAY.
- A sheer-following bulwark is a swept curve and belongs to `edges[]`/sheer_band.
Quantising it to the grid would step the one curve the whole fleet was rebuilt to draw.
- A CONTINUOUS fall across a run of several wall panels cannot be exact. A panel's top
drops a whole eighth-cell or nothing, so a 0.25 m fall shared between four panels has
to be dealt out in two lumps of 0.125; the run is then a chord of the true plane and
departs from it by up to 0.05 m on the trawler. Making it exact needs a 1/64 m lift
step - 33 entries to distribute one number - and that is CAD wearing a stepper.
- A wall's FOOT is level. A deckhouse standing on a falling deck sits on the mean of the
deck under it, inside the deck plate's own 0.13 m.
- NO PIECE CUTS A DECK. `deck_tile` and `roof_slope` are rectangles, so a roof laid over a
chamfered casing overhangs the chamfer by span*0.354 m - 0.35 m at span 1, 2.83 m at
span 8. In PLAN a chamfered casing therefore reads as a perfect rectangle, and in profile
a chamfer is invisible because it is a plan feature. `corner_45` only reads from a low
three-quarter angle. A chamfered deck piece is the honest fix and it does not exist.
- A DOOR NEEDS A PANEL 2.18 m TALL IN v, so `height 4` (2.00 m) cannot carry one and says
so, in words. The kit's door gives 2.10 m of clear head above the panel's own FOOT, which
is what it can promise: it cannot see what the piece next door lays underfoot. It does
allow for the worst floor the kit itself can lay AT THE SAME NODE - a `heavy` deck_tile,
0.150 m of walking surface above the node - but a sole `lift`ed off its node, or a wall
`lift`ed down into one, is a relationship BETWEEN two placements and no constraint in this
file can see it. Constraints are within a piece.
- A concave corner carries NO rake transition, and no piece does (see corner_45).
- A `roof_slope` prism has open triangular ends. There is no gusset in the kit, so a
breakwater built as slope + after face is two triangles of daylight; `roof_slope` is a
VISOR here, which is a cantilevered plate and has no ends to close.

pieces.description: One plate of a deckhouse side, plumb or raked, level-topped or falling, optionally with a door, a window or a scuttle punched through it. The workhorse: everything that is not a corner, a window band, a deck or a trim run is this.

span._is: length of the run. Six standard widths, the way a merchant sells plate.

height._is: 1.0 m to 3.0 m in whole cells. 5 cells = 2.5 m is a tier; 2 cells = 1.0 m is a bulwark or a coaming course. `head` trims it finer.

head._is: 0.125 m steps ADDED to the top of `height`, so a tier can be 2.75 m (height 5, head 2) without the placement lattice leaving whole cells. Separate from `height` because changing what `height` counts would silently resize every deckhouse already saved.

rake._is: how far the TOP edge stands outboard of the foot, in 0.125 m steps. Positive rakes out (a trawler's front), negative tumbles home (a side). At the 2.5 m tier height this spans -21.8 to +21.8 degrees, which covers every rake in the fleet, and the step is half what version 1 could say.

fall._is: how far the top edge DROPS from the start of the run to its end, in 0.125 m steps. The foot stays level. This is the wall under a falling deck; a positive fall drops the far end, a negative one raises it. HOW A FALLING RUN CHAINS, exactly: the next panel takes the drop out of its `head`, which counts the same unit, and then head AND foot both close. Taking it out of `lift` instead closes the head and opens the FOOT by the same 0.125*fall, because lift moves the whole piece. Two panels at the same `fall` and the same `head` do not form one plane either - they make a sawtooth. `fall` is a drop over ONE piece, not a slope.

lift._is: moves the whole piece up off its grid node in 0.125 m steps, +-0.5 m. What lets a wall stand on a deck that is not on a whole cell.

opening._is: a real hole with its proud casing, centred on the panel. A door is 1.20 m wide and gives 2.10 m of CLEAR VERTICAL HEAD above the panel's foot; a window 0.80 x 0.70 at 1.20 m sill; a scuttle 0.40 x 0.40. The opening is the piece, not a set of four numbers - which is why span is fixed by what fits, not by the hole, and why `constraints` refuses a hole the panel is too narrow or too short to carry. WHY A DOOR IS 1.20 m AND NOT THE 0.85 m A HOUSE DOOR IS, measured rather than chosen: the thing that walks through it is not a person, it is `scenes/shared/player.tscn` - a capsule of RADIUS 0.35, so 0.70 m across the shoulders where a person is 0.45. At 0.85 m the clear column left for the capsule's centre line was 0.13 m wide, and `piece_interior_test` reported every doorway in every piece-built deckhouse as impassable. Every hand-authored deckhouse in this repo had already been widened to 1.10-2.00 m by the same measurement on the same figure (`plan_interior_test`, `demo_workboat`); the kit was the one authoring layer still quoting the real-world number. WHY THE HEAD IS 2.10 m AND NOT THE 1.95 m IT WAS, every term measured on a spawned vessel through PhysicsServer3D: 1.80 m of player, plus 0.150 m for the thickest sole the kit can lay at the same node (a `heavy` deck_tile is 0.30 m thick and its plate is centred on the node, so you walk on 0.150 m of it), plus 0.052 m for the COLLIDER HANG (a casing slab's box is fitted to the slab plus and minus half its 0.20 m thickness ALONG THE PLATE NORMAL, and a raked plate's normal tilts, so the lintel's box hangs below the lintel you can see - 0.052 m measured at rake 8, 0.022 m at rake 2), leaves 0.098 m. The old 1.95 m paid for the player and the hull's own plating and nothing else, and at rake 4 it had already stopped paying for the player. 2.10 rather than 2.05 costs NOTHING: `height*0.5+head*0.125` lands on the 0.125 m lattice, and there is no panel rise between the 2.13 m one target needs and the 2.18 m the other does.

derived._is: NAMED ONCE, USED TWICE. `door_h` is the opening's height ALONG THE PLATE SURFACE and it is also what the constraint below subtracts from the plate to decide whether the hole fits. Written out twice those two drift, and a drifted constraint goes on passing while it stops guarding the clamp it was written for.

constraints._is: a hole needs a panel wide enough to carry it AND to keep plating either side of it. A 1.20 m door wants 3 cells (0.15 m of plating each side), a 0.80 m window 2, a 0.40 m scuttle 1. Without this the baker CLAMPS the opening to what fits - a span-2 panel with a door quietly became a 1.00 m hole with no plating at all - and a kit whose pieces quietly change size is worse than one that refuses.

AND TALL ENOUGH. The constraint above relates the hole to `span` alone, and `span` is the one thing that does not set the plate's v-length: `height`, `head`, `rake` and `fall` all do. Over the 91,800 legal settings that punch a hole, 19,742 - 21.5% - had that hole silently CUT DOWN by the baker (`plate_openings` clamps to `ref.y - sill`), and 27,916 lost or trimmed a casing member. A `height 2` panel with a `door` asked for 1.20 x 1.95 and got 1.20 x 1.00 with no lintel; a `height 2` window got 0.80 x 0.000. The 0.08 is PLATE_FRAME_WIDTH minus SKIN_EPS - the lintel laps the plating by exactly that much and vanishes below it - and 1.98 / 1.78 are sill + height + that lap for the window and the scuttle. A raked plate is LONGER in v than it is tall, which is why this is measured against `v_plate` and not against `height`.

A DOOR'S HEAD IS A LINTEL YOU WALK UNDER AND IT HAS TO READ AS LEVEL. An opening's head is a line of constant v, and in a FALLING panel constant v drops with the top edge - at fall 4 across a span-3 panel the head falls 0.26 m over the door's own 1.20 m, which is a ramp, not a lintel. `door_h` already keeps the LOWEST corner of that head 2.10 m clear, so the door is still passable; what this refuses is the one that looks broken. The bound is the panel's own 0.10 m plating, the same 'displaced by less than the material it is made of' test the 0.125 m trim step was chosen on. Gentle falls survive: fall 1 at span 6, fall 3 at span 8.

door._is: MEASURED ALONG THE PLATE, NOT UP THE WALL. An opening's sill and height are lengths on the plate surface, so on a wall raked r over a rise h a 1.95 m hole is only 1.95*h/sqrt(h*h+r*r) tall in the world - 1.81 m at rake 8, which a 1.80 m player cannot walk through once the collider and the deck under their feet are counted. `door_h` divides that factor back out, so the head is 2.10 m above the panel's foot at every rake the stepper offers instead of at one of them.

pieces.description: A wheelhouse or saloon wall carrying a RIBBON WINDOW: a coaming course, a dark glass plate set 90 mm into the reveal, a header above it and mullions standing in the reveal. One piece, four to seven plates. A ribbon is not a row of holes - the ferry proved that the hard way - so it is a different piece from a punched window, not a parameter of one.

head._is: 0.125 m steps added to the top, the same trim `wall_panel` carries, so a glazed wall in a 2.75 m tier is flush with the plated wall beside it.

rake._is: the whole wall rakes, and the coaming, glass, header and mullions all lean with it - the band follows the wall rather than sitting on it. 0.125 m steps.

fall._is: drops the far end of the HEADER's top edge, in 0.125 m steps, so a glazed wall can follow a falling roofline. The coaming and the glass band stay level, which is what a wheelhouse actually looks like: the roof falls aft and the windows do not.

sill._is: coaming height under the glass. 2 cells = 1.0 m, which is the fall-barrier dimension the 1.8 m figure sets.

lights._is: panes across the run. lights-1 mullions, evenly spaced, 0.10 m wide IN METRES - authored as a fraction of the plate they came out 3 m wide on a ferry and the band read as portholes.

constraints._is: sill 3 and band 3 in a 4-cell wall are two legal picks that leave no header, and a zero-height header is a degenerate quad. At least one cell of wall must stand above the glass.

the header has to survive the fall. A 0.5 m header that falls 0.5 m is a triangle at one end and a zero-height quad at the other, and the baker refuses to draw it - so the piece refuses first, in its own words.

pieces.description: THE PIECE THAT BEATS BLOCKINESS, AND THE ONLY DIAGONAL WALL. A 45-degree chord across a corner of `span` cells. In `chain: corner` its two vertical edges belong to the two AXIS walls that meet there, so it closes the wedge that opens when a raked wall meets a wall raked differently - the plate is bilinear and a twisted quad is exactly what it is for. In `chain: run` both edges belong to 45-degree NEIGHBOURS instead, which is what makes a raked diagonal wall run close. At span 1 it is a 0.71 m knuckle on a deckhouse corner; at span 8 it is a 5.66 m bow facet.

span._is: cells in X and in Z. The chord is span*0.707 m, so 8 cells is a 5.66 m facet - a ferry's bow, not a knuckle. The cap was 4 for no reason anyone wrote down.

chain._is: WHICH TWO WALLS THIS FACET'S EDGES BELONG TO, and getting it wrong is a slot of daylight. `corner` (the default, and byte-identical to version 1) hands each top corner to an AXIS wall, so it moves along that wall's own outboard normal - one along -X, one along -Z. `run` hands both to 45-degree NEIGHBOURS, so both move along the FACET's normal, 0.125*rake/sqrt2 in each of X and Z. A chain of `corner` facets closes only when every rake is 0: the gap at the head is 0.125*sqrt(rake_a^2+rake_b^2), which is 0.177 m at one step and 1.414 m at eight, and a raked bow facet longer than one piece was plumb in the middle with a vertical crease every 5.66 m. A chain of `run` facets at one rake closes to the bit.

head._is: 0.125 m of extra height, matching the walls it joins. A facet at a different head from its neighbours opens a slot exactly that wide.

rake_a._is: the rake of the wall meeting this facet on the -Z side, in 0.125 m steps. Must equal that wall's own rake or a slot opens.

rake_b._is: the rake of the wall meeting this facet on the -X side.

fall._is: drops the -Z end of the top edge, the same way a wall panel's fall does, so a facet in a falling run hands the next piece the height it ended at.

constraints._is: the -Z top corner has to stay outboard of the foot corner it is diagonally across from. Past that it crosses it and the quad ties itself in a bow - 109 settings of the full (span, height, rake_a, rake_b, fall) cross product did exactly that and NOTHING named them; the baker refused them as `self-crossing quad` and the piece said nothing. A refusal in the piece's own words is the difference between `you cannot do that` and a hole.
the same for the -X top corner.

run._is: 0.08838834764831845 is 0.125/sqrt(2): the rake is still a whole eighth-cell MEASURED PERPENDICULAR TO THE WALL, and on a 45-degree wall that lands as equal parts in X and in Z. The player's number is a grid count; the irrational is the same irrational the chord already carries.

pieces.description: A horizontal plate - a deck, a tier roof, a boat deck, a funnel cap - flat, or FALLING in 0.125 m steps so a roof drains and a boat deck is not dead level. Placed on the grid at its own level and NOT derived from the walls underneath it: deriving it is what a room was, and a room made every deckhouse a shed. Because the raked walls of a tier land off-grid at the top, the deck laid over them is normally one cell larger all round, and the overhang that results is the EAVE. Two tiles at the same fall, back to back off a centreline, make a CAMBER rather than a slope.

fall._is: the far edge (+Z in the piece frame, away from the outward face) drops this many 0.125 m steps below the near edge. It is a DROP and not an angle, so the slope a tile ends up with is the drop over its own depth: 2 steps over 16 cells is 0.25 m in 8 m, 1.8 degrees, which is a boat deck; 2 steps over 4 cells is 7.1 degrees, which is a hood. `facing` points it at any of four quarters, and 0 is the flat deck version 1 had.

lift._is: moves the tile up off its grid node in 0.125 m steps. What chains a falling deck: the next tile down-slope carries the lift its neighbour's fall ended at, and because both are counted in the same unit the two edges are identical.

gauge._is: 0.08 / 0.13 / 0.30 m. A light gauge is a visor or a hood, deck is what you walk on, heavy is a funnel cap or a bulwark capping.

pieces.description: A roof or casing top that climbs `rise` WHOLE CELLS over its `depth`. Chains with itself: put the next one `rise` cells higher and the two are one continuous slope. This is a whaleback, a machinery-casing top, a wheelhouse visor, a companionway hood. Its rise stays in whole cells on purpose - the chaining is the point, and a gentle drainage fall is `deck_tile`'s `fall`, not a finer rise here. It is NOT a wall_panel lying down - a wall's extent is vertical and a slope's is horizontal, and conflating them makes both harder to place.

lift._is: 0.125 m steps off the grid node, so a slope can start on a deck that is itself off the lattice.

pieces.description: The thin proud stuff, and it earns its place because without it every joint in the kit is a bare intersection of two planes, which is half of what 'blocky' means. Four profiles off one run: an eave under a deck edge, a cap over a bulwark, a coaming lip standing on a deck, a rubbing strake on a wall. Trim is where a build stops looking printed.

offset._is: moves the run outboard (positive) or INBOARD (negative) in 0.125 m steps. A trim run has no height and therefore cannot carry a rake, so a strake crossing a RAKED wall is set out to meet the wall at the height it is placed - the same eighth-cell arithmetic the rake itself uses. It was 0..8 until a critic measured the other half: a wall that TUMBLES HOME leans inboard, and at rake -8 the daylight between a strake at offset 0 and the plating is 0.055 m at half a metre up, 0.155 at a metre and 0.355 at two. No shipped fixture carried a strake on a tumblehome wall, which is the only reason a one-directional parameter survived with an `_is` claiming it solved both.

lift._is: 0.125 m steps off the grid node, so a cap rail lands on a deck that is off the lattice.

eave._is: a flat lip standing 0.30 m outboard under a deck edge

cap._is: a 0.36 m cap rail lying over a bulwark or a coaming

coaming._is: a 0.25 m lip standing up off a deck edge

strake._is: a 0.22 m band proud of a wall face
